profile.summary: Exodus presents God's answer to the central questions of faith: how a relationship is established with Him, what this relationship requires and how to remain in it. The book shows that Israel needed not only liberation from slavery in Egypt, but also to the exit of sin and entry into communion with the Lord. Thus, Exodus unites redemption, covenant, and divine presence: God frees his people, reveals who He is in Sinai and provides for the tabernacle to dwell among them.
profile.setting: The historical scene lies the exit of Egypt between 1450 and 1250 BC, in a period when Egypt was a first-order military and cultural power, especially during the 18th dynasty. The introduction emphasizes that Israel came out when Egyptian power was at its peak, not in a time of weakness. As for authorship, tradition attributes the book to Moses, but this authorship is debated by many scholars. On the date of the Exodus, the source presents two main proposals: an ancient date, around 1446 BC, and a later date, around 1270 BC; the question remains uncertain, although there are biblical and archaeological arguments for both positions.

structure.label: Livramento of Egypt
structure.description: The liberation of the Hebrews from slavery and the exit from the land of Egypt.

structure.label: Revelation in Sinai and Covenant
structure.description: God teaches who He is and how the life of his people should be under the covenant.

structure.label: Tabernacle and presence of God
structure.description: The provision of the sanctuary that Israel may live in the holy presence of the Lord.

themes: God frees his people from slavery
The covenant reveals the holy and ethical character of God
Relationship with God requires fidelity and obedience
The presence of God is the ultimate goal of redemption
readingKeys: Notice the progression of the book: exit, covenant, and presence; the Exodus does not end in liberation.
Note that the commandments and demands of the covenant deal with much of the relationships between people, not just of worship.
Read the tabernacle as the central part of the book's message: it shows God's purpose to dwell with his people.
profile.cautions: The introduction does not treat Exodus as a simple narrative of escape, but as a history of redemption and communion. It is also important to remember that the date of the Exodus and the Mosaic authorship are debated questions; the source presents arguments for more than one possibility without definitively resolving the subject.

dossier.narratedEra: Exodus's narrative is set in Egypt from the imperial period, with Israel's departure from some points between 1450 and 1250 BC. The sources associate this background with the eighteenth Egyptian dynasty (1550-1295 BC), to the height of the pharaonic power and the transition of the people of Israel from slavery to the alliance in Sinai and to the divine presence in the tabernacle.
dossier.compositionEra: The sources do not fix a composition date for Exodus. They preserve the traditional mosaic authorship for the Pentateuch, although they note that many scholars question it. Matthew Henry treats Moses as the writer of the book; Tyndale's introduction mentions the Mosaic tradition, but does not provide a safe chronology of writing.

politics.title: Egypt as imperial power on the horizon of the Exodus
politics.detail: The introduction describes Egypt as the great military and cultural power of the moment, especially under the eighteenth dynasty, with expansion to Canaan and south of the Nile. This helps to read the Exodus as a confrontation between the God of Israel and an empire at the height, not as an escape from a weakened state.
politics.readingImpact: Divine liberation gains political weight: God acts against the maximum power of the time, showing that the exodus does not depend on the Egyptian weakness, but on the sovereignty of the Lord.

politics.title: The dynasty exchange and suspicion against the Semites
politics.detail: Ex 1:8 is read as a sign of the arrival of a new dynasty. The notes relate the "new king who did not know Joseph" to the expulsion of the Hyksos around 1540 BC and the subsequent suspicion against Semitic foreigners, including the Israelites.
politics.readingImpact: The verse ceases to be just a narrative detail and begins to mark a political turn: the old favor becomes state distrust and systemic oppression.

politics.title: Pharaoh as title and the power hierarchy
politics.detail: The notes recall that "fara" is title, not personal name, and highlight the contrast between the king and the midwives: military power, prestige and wealth on one side; slavery and vulnerability on the other. Even so, the midwives resist.
politics.readingImpact: Reading highlights that obedience to God can occur amid an overwhelming political structure; the text values the fidelity of the weak before the state.

politics.title: The treaty of the alliance as a political form
politics.detail: Exodus 2023 is described as molded according to the structure of treaties of suerania-vasaweage of the ancient Near East: preamble, historical prologue, stipulations, written preservation, witnesses and blessings and curses. God adopts this form to formalize his relationship with the people.
politics.readingImpact: This shows that the covenant in Sinai is not only religious; it organizes the national life of Israel under the rule of the God-King.

politics.title: Rulers reminded for the chronology: Shishaque, Solomon and Ramses II
politics.detail: The introduction uses the sack of Judah by Shishaque (1Rs 14:25-26) as an external fixed point to retreat in the chronological calculus. In the late hypothesis, the exodus would fit into the early reign of Ramses II, and the name of the city of Ramesses is linked to that pharaoh.
politics.readingImpact: The book is read in dialogue with kings and royal dynasties, but the proposed dates remain a reconstruction and not a simple given of the biblical text.
politics.reference: Exodus Introduction, The Date of the Exodus

customs.title: Forced work and building materials in the Nile delta
customs.detail: Ex 1:11-14 is explained on the basis of Egyptian construction practices: stone came mainly from the south, while in the north predominated clay bricks with straw or shells as binder. Pithom and Ramesses appear as centers linked to this work.
customs.readingImpact: The text gains social concreteness: oppression is not abstract, but involves production, mortar, furnace, captivity and an economic system that exploits enslaved labor.

customs.title: Midwives, birth and birth control
customs.detail: The notes treat Sifrá and Puá as representatives of a larger group of midwives and observe that the warrant of killing the boys would preserve the Egyptian workforce while mining the Hebrew cohesion. The comment also notes the possible reference to a childbirth stone or the act of observing the baby at the time of birth.
customs.readingImpact: The narrative becomes a portrait of state violence about the family and the female body, and the fear of God appears in the domestic space of childbirth.

customs.title: Patriarchal family, migration and livelihood in times of hunger
customs.detail: The introduction recalls that Jacob and his family went to Egypt because of a severe drought and a grain supply previously stored by Joseph. The book therefore begins with a migrant family that seeks survival before becoming enslaved people.
customs.readingImpact: The domestic backdrop explains why the exodus is not only a geographical change, but the transformation of a patriarchal house into a nation.

customs.title: Saturday, rest and life of covenant
customs.detail: The notes say that the Sabbath is sanctified when it is dedicated to the Lord and that this rest reminds that the sustenance comes from the grace of God, not just from human labor. The commandment is read as a community practice of trust.
customs.readingImpact: The observance of the Sabbath is seen as a reorientation of the economy of time: Israel must live as dependent people, not as self-sufficient people.

customs.title: Worship without images and without ritual eroticization
customs.detail: In Ex 20:22-26, the notes observe that the altar should be of unwashed earth or stones and that the exposure of nudity could separate Israel from cananeyan practices linked to the cult of fertility. In Ex 40, the tabernacle is the place where God speaks and dwells with the people.
customs.readingImpact: The Israeli cult is presented as distinct from the religious environment around: no molded idols, without magic manipulation and without sexual rituals.

language.title: "exodus " as "exit."
language.detail: Matthew Henry notes that the Greek translators called Exodus' book because he begins with the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt. Tyndale's introduction also defines exodos as the way out.
language.readingImpact: The title already interprets the book: history is not only about political liberation, but about the passage of a state of oppression to a new relationship with God.

language.title: The Ten Words and Not Arbitrary Commandments
language.detail: Ex 20:1 is explained as "all these words," and the notes observe that Hebrew calls this set of "Ten Words." They are presented as the Creator's basic instructions for human life, not as arbitrary demands.
language.readingImpact: This reinforces the pastoral reading of the Decalogue as the wisdom of creation and not as a mere legalistic list.

language.title: Name of God, character and reverence
language.detail: In Ex 20:7, the notes say that the name, in Hebrew, communicates nature and character. To take in vain the name of God includes making it insignificant, as by false oaths, but the principle is broader than that.
language.readingImpact: The commandment deals not only with pronunciation, but of reputation, truth and public representation of the God of Israel.

language.title: Love and hate as choice of alliance
language.detail: Notes of "x 20:5-6 explain that in biblical language, "amar" and "odiar" involve decision and action, not just feeling. The contrast helps to understand the unique fidelity requested by God.
language.readingImpact: The covenant is read as concrete loyalty; devotion is not only religious emotion, but direction of life.

language.title: "Hebreu" as a derogatory social term
language.detail: "x 1:15 notes that the origin of the term "hebreu" is uncertain and that Egyptians and Philistines apparently used it as a pejorative label for a subaltern group.
language.readingImpact: This shows that Israel's identity was also a social identity marked by external contempt, not just a neutral ethnic designation.

language.title: The present and the written presence of the covenant
language.detail: In "x 40:3, the Hebrew translated "alliance" is explained as "eduth," "testemunho," referring especially to the stipulations. The copy written in the ark served as a testimony of the covenant.
language.readingImpact: The language emphasizes that the covenant is not vague: it has content, memory and material record within the sanctuary.

timeline.title: General window for exodus: 1450-1250 BC
timeline.detail: The introduction places the exodus at some point between 1450 and 1250 BC, without fixing the exact year. The wide range reflects the uncertainty of chronological reconstructions.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader should avoid dealing with any single date as right; the book predates our attempts at absolute synchronization.

timeline.title: Hyksos, expulsion and the XVIII dynasty
timeline.detail: The notes place the Hyksos in power of northern Egypt from about 1650 to 1550 BC, with expulsion around 1540 BC, followed by the XVIII dynasty and Ahmose (1550-1525 BC).
timeline.readingImpact: This scenario helps to understand why a new king could distrust the Israelites and reinterpret their presence as a political threat.

timeline.title: The Merneptá Stela as an external landmark
timeline.detail: The introduction cites the stela of Merneptá, dated about 1209 BC, as Israel's first clear record outside the Bible and as relevant to the Israeli presence in southern Palestine.
timeline.readingImpact: This milestone serves as a point of contact between Bible and archaeology, although it does not solve the date of the exodus alone.
timeline.reference: Exodus Introduction, The Date of the Exodus

timeline.title: Ancient hypothesis: exodus around 1446 BC.
timeline.detail: The traditional reading links 1Rs 6:1 to 480 years between the exodus and the beginning of Solomon's temple in 967 BC, resulting in an approximate date of 1446 BC and an entrance to Canaan around 1406 BC. The notes also mention Amarna's letters and the testimony of Judges 11:26 as arguments compatible with this proposal.
timeline.readingImpact: If this chronology is followed, the Exodus narrative fits into a longer historical line, with the conquest and the period of the judges occurring earlier.
timeline.reference: Introduction of Exodus, The Date of the Exodus (Early Exodus)

timeline.title: Late hypothesis: exodus around 1270 BC.
timeline.detail: The late alternative places the exodus about 300 years before 967 BC, at the beginning of the reign of Ramses II (1279-1213 BC), and relates the city of Ramesses to this pharaoh. The proposal also calls for archaeological evidence of construction and settlement in the late 13th century BC.
timeline.readingImpact: In this reading, Ex 1:11 receives a framework closer to the ramessid period, but the proposal depends on a different chronology for 1Rs 6:1.
timeline.reference: Exodus, Exodus Introduction, The Date of the Exodus (Late Exodus)

investigation: The introduction offers two competing chronologies for the exodus, but does not decide between them.
The Mosaic authorship is affirmed as tradition, while the essay does not receive specific dating in the sources.
The notes use archaeology and inscriptions as interpretive support, not as definitive independent proof.
There are clear devotional and confessional readings; even so, historical and philological observations are useful for contextual study.
Some details, such as the relationship between 1Rs 6:1 and 480 years or the value of Amarna's cards, remain debated in the notes themselves.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends only on the annexed notes of Tyndale and Matthew Henry, who are selective and have pastoral/explanatory, non-encyclopedic purpose. Therefore, several important themes of Exodus receive little or no coverage: detailed Egyptian administration, food daily life, complete family structure, developing Israeli cult, and textual issues beyond 12:40. The composition of the book is not safely dated in the sources; the Mosaic tradition is affirmed, but not demonstrated. The proposed dates for the exodus and patriarchal chronology are presented as reconstructions debated, not as historical certainties. Nor should these notes be read as independent archaeological evidence: they themselves speak of possible evidence, compatibility and alternative scenarios.
